{{Short description|Result in social choice theory}}{{Electoral systems sidebar|expanded=Social and collective choice}}

The '''McKelvey–Schofield chaos theorem''' is a result in [[social choice theory]]. It states that if preferences are defined over a multidimensional policy space, then choosing policies using [[majority rule]] is unstable. There will in most cases be no [[Condorcet winner]] and any policy can be enacted through a sequence of votes, regardless of the original policy. This means that adding more policies and changing the order of votes ("agenda manipulation") can be used to arbitrarily pick the winner.<ref name=":0" />

Versions of the theorem have been proved for different types of preferences, with different classes of exceptions. A version of the theorem was first proved by [[Richard McKelvey]] in 1976, for preferences based on [[Euclidean distance|Euclidean distances]] in <math>\mathbb{R}^{n}</math>. Another version of the theorem was proved by [[Norman Schofield]] in 1978, for [[Differentiable function|differentiable]] preferences.

The theorem can be thought of as showing that [[Arrow's impossibility theorem]] holds when preferences are restricted to be [[Concave function|concave]] in <math>\mathbb{R}^{n}</math>. The [[median voter theorem]] shows that when preferences are restricted to be single-peaked on the real line, Arrow's theorem does not hold, and the median voter's ideal point is a Condorcet winner. In higher dimensions the median voter's ideal point can be found by the [[geometric median]].<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Weiszfeld | first1 = E. | last2 = Plastria | first2 = Frank | author2-link = Frank Plastria | date = April 2008 | doi = 10.1007/s10479-008-0352-z | issue = 1 | journal = [[Annals of Operations Research]] | pages = 7–41 | title = On the point for which the sum of the distances to {{mvar|n}} given points is minimum | volume = 167| s2cid = 21000317 }}</ref>

== Definitions ==
The theorem considers a finite number of voters, {{mvar|n}}, who vote for policies which are represented as points in [[Euclidean space]] of dimension {{mvar|m}}. Each vote is between two policies using [[majority rule]]. Each voter, {{mvar|i}}, has a [[utility function]], {{mvar|U<sub>i</sub>}}, which measures how much they value different policies.{{clarify|date=August 2024|reason=Ties could happen if utilities are equal or there are an even number of voters}}

== Euclidean preferences ==
[[Richard McKelvey]] considered the case when preferences are "Euclidean metrics".<ref>{{cite journal |last1=McKelvey |first1=Richard D. |title=Intransitivities in Multidimensional Voting Models and Some Implications for Agenda Control |journal=Journal of Economic Theory |date=June 1976 |volume=12 |issue=3 |pages=472–482|doi=10.1016/0022-0531(76)90040-5 }}</ref>  That means every voter's utility function has the form
<math display=block>
U_i(x)=\Phi_i \cdot d(x,x_i)
</math>
for all policies {{mvar|x}} and some {{mvar|x<sub>i</sub>}}, where {{mvar|d}} is the [[Euclidean distance]] and <math>\Phi_i</math> is a [[monotone decreasing]] function.

Under these conditions, there could be a collection of policies which don't have a [[Condorcet winner]] using majority rule. This means that, given a number of policies {{mvar|X<sub>a</sub>}},  {{mvar|X<sub>b</sub>}}, {{mvar|X<sub>c</sub>}}, there could be a series of pairwise elections where:
# {{mvar|X<sub>a</sub>}} wins over {{mvar|X<sub>b</sub>}}
# {{mvar|X<sub>b</sub>}} wins over {{mvar|X<sub>c</sub>}}
# {{mvar|X<sub>c</sub>}} wins over {{mvar|X<sub>a</sub>}}

McKelvey proved that elections can be even more "chaotic" than that: If there is no equilibrium outcome{{clarify|date=August 2024|reason=Definition?}} then any two policies, e.g. {{mvar|A}} and {{mvar|B}}, have a sequence of policies, <math>X_1,X_2,...,X_s</math>, where each one pairwise wins over the other in a series of elections, meaning:
# {{mvar|A}} wins over {{mvar|X<sub>1</sub>}}
# {{mvar|X<sub>1</sub>}} wins over {{mvar|X<sub>2</sub>}}
# ...
# {{mvar|X<sub>s</sub>}} wins over {{mvar|B}}

This is true regardless of whether {{mvar|A}} would beat {{mvar|B}} or ''vice versa''.

=== Example ===
[[File:McKelvey theorem example.svg|thumb|An example of McKelvey's theorem]]

The simplest illustrating example is in [[Euclidean plane|two dimensions]], with three voters. Each voter will then have a maximum preferred policy, and any other policy will have a corresponding circular [[indifference curve]] centered at the preferred policy. If a policy was proposed, then any policy in [[Circle–circle intersection|the intersection]] of two voters indifference curves would beat it. Any point in the plane will almost always have a set of points that are preferred by 2 out of 3 voters.

== Generalisations ==
[[Norman Schofield]] extended the theorem to more general classes of utility functions, requiring only that they are [[Differentiable function|differentiable]]. He also established conditions for the existence of a directed [[continuous path]] of policies, where each policy further along the path would win against one earlier.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Schofield |first1=N.|title=Instability of Simple Dynamic Games |journal=The Review of Economic Studies |date=1 October 1978 |volume=45 |issue=3 |pages=575–594 |doi=10.2307/2297259|jstor=2297259 }}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last1=Cox |first1=Gary W. |author-link=Gary W. Cox |title=Positive Changes in Political Science |last2=Shepsle |first2=Kenneth A. |author-link2=Kenneth Shepsle |pages=20–23 |chapter=Majority Cycling and Agenda Manipulation: Richard McKelvey's Contributions and Legacy |date=2007 |publisher=University of Michigan Press |isbn=978-0-472-06986-6 |editor-last=Aldrich |editor-first=John Herbert |series=Analytical perspectives on politics |location=Ann Arbor, Michigan |editor-last2=Alt |editor-first2=James E. |editor-last3=Lupia |editor-first3=Arthur}}</ref> Some of Schofield's proofs were later found to be incorrect by Jeffrey S. Banks, who corrected his proofs.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Banks |first=Jeffrey S. |date=1995-01-01 |title=Singularity theory and core existence in the spatial model |journal=Journal of Mathematical Economics |volume=24 |issue=6 |pages=523–536 |doi=10.1016/0304-4068(94)00704-E |issn=0304-4068|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Saari |first=Donald G. |author-link=Donald G. Saari |url=https://www.worldcat.org/title/227031682 |title=Disposing dictators, demystifying voting paradoxes: social choice analysis |date=2008 |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] |isbn=978-0-521-51605-1 |location=Cambridge, New York |chapter=Deliver Us from the Plurality Vote |oclc=227031682}}</ref>
